short_summary: Discover the historic Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel in Snowdonia, which served as the British base camp for the legendary 1953 Everest expedition.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: The Welsh mountain inn that helped conquer Everest

paragraphs: In the early hours of 2 June 1953, guests staying at the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel in the heart of Eryri, also known as Snowdonia, were abruptly awakened by excited footsteps rushing down the hallway. According to reports, this commotion was followed by joyful shouts and the distinct sound of champagne corks popping. A late-night telephone call had just confirmed that Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay had successfully conquered Mount Everest. Remarkably, this historic milestone coincided with the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II later that same day, catapulting the two mountaineers onto front pages across the globe. For decades, however, the narrative largely credited Hillary while marginalising Tenzing Norgay, an indigenous Sherpa and vital load-carrying guide. A new film titled Tenzing, released on Apple TV and starring Genden Phuntsok alongside Tom Hiddleston, aims to rectify this historical imbalance by highlighting Tenzing's own profound ambitions and extensive climbing experience.

A full year prior to the triumphant British expedition, Tenzing and Swiss climber Raymond Lambert had already ascended to unprecedented heights, reaching a new altitude record before a brutal storm and dwindling oxygen forced them to retreat less than 250 metres from the summit. Meanwhile, back in the United Kingdom, Colonel John Hunt was appointed by the Joint Himalayan Committee to assemble the official team. He established the primary base camp at the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel, situated at the foot of the Llanberis Pass. Within these rugged surroundings, the team practiced technical climbing techniques and rigorously tested revolutionary equipment, including closed-circuit oxygen tanks and specialized high-altitude boots designed to withstand the lethal temperatures of the death zone above 8,000 metres.

Today, the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel operates as a living time capsule, preserving the authentic atmosphere of those pioneering days. Still managed by the founder Christopher Briggs's grandsons, Nick and Rupert Pullee, the property deliberately avoids modern distractions like televisions or background music, retaining instead its classic charm, cozy rooms, and roaring fires. Inside a glass display case in the public areas, visitors can inspect original artefacts from the 1953 expedition, such as goggles, an ice axe, a compass, and an extraordinary ledger containing the fingerprints of Sherpas who could neither read nor write. The walls of the Smoke Room are adorned with historical photographs, including images of Tenzing sharing tea with young expedition members.

The hotel also maintains unique traditions, such as the Snowdon Club, where young visitors who successfully climb Yr Wyddfa are tested on their mountain knowledge, rewarded with a silver ice-axe brooch, and permitted to drink lemonade from Hillary's pewter tankard. Dining at the hotel remains a traditional affair announced by the striking of a gong, serving hearty meals like roast Welsh lamb and steak and ale pies. With its signed ceilings in the Everest Room and walls covered in rich mountaineering history, the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel continues to offer travelers a rare opportunity to step back in time amidst the wild landscapes of Wales.

facts.fact: On 2 June 1953, guests at the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel in Eryri (Snowdonia) were woken by news that Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay had successfully summited Mount Everest.
The Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel served as the British base camp for the 1953 Everest expedition led by Colonel John Hunt.
A new film titled Tenzing, starring Genden Phuntsok and Tom Hiddleston, is released on Apple TV to re-examine Tenzing Norgay's pivotal role and personal dreams.
In spring 1952, Tenzing and Swiss climber Raymond Lambert reached an altitude record, coming within 250 metres of the Everest summit before retreating.
The hotel preserves original expedition artefacts, including goggles, an ice axe, a compass, and a ledger of Sherpas' fingerprints.
The Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel is run by Christopher Briggs's grandsons, Nick and Rupert Pullee, maintaining its vintage character and traditions like the Snowdon Club.
